questions.statement: Which of the following statements about constructors is correct?

options.text: Every constructor must return the newly created object.
A constructor must return `void`.
Constructors do not have a return type.
A constructor's return type must match the class name.

questions.explanation: Constructors have no return type at all, not even `void`. They run automatically to initialise the new object.

questions.statement: A constructor without parameters is referred to as a _______ constructor.

options.text: default
copy
conversion
delegating

questions.explanation: A constructor that can be called without arguments is the default constructor.

questions.statement: A class defines at least one constructor, but no parameterless constructor. What happens when code tries to create an object without providing arguments?

options.text: The compiler supplies zero values for every constructor parameter.
The object is created without running a constructor.
The compiler automatically generates a default constructor despite the user-defined constructor.
The compiler issues an error message.

questions.explanation: Once a class declares any constructor, the compiler stops generating the implicit default constructor, so creating an object without arguments is a compile error.

questions.statement: What is the syntax for declaring a destructor in a class named `class_name`?

options.text: `class_name~();`
`~class_name(void);`
`void ~class_name();`
`delete class_name();`

questions.explanation: A destructor is `~` plus the class name, with no return type and no parameters. `(void)` is just an explicitly empty parameter list.

questions.statement: Why is it impossible to overload a destructor?

options.text: A destructor must be declared `static`.
Destructors do not have any parameters.
A class can have only one data member.
Destructors are inherited but cannot be declared by a class.

questions.explanation: Overloads need different parameter lists. A destructor never takes parameters, so a class can only have one destructor.

questions.statement: In what order are an object's individual data members destroyed?

options.text: In the order in which they were declared.
In alphabetical order by member name.
All data members are destroyed simultaneously.
In the order opposite to the order in which they were created.

questions.explanation: Members are constructed in declaration order and destroyed in the reverse order: last constructed, first destroyed.

questions.statement: When is a destructor called automatically for a local object that does not have static storage duration?

options.text: At the end of the code block defining the object.
Immediately after the object's constructor returns.
Only when the program explicitly calls `delete`.
At the end of the entire program, regardless of the object's scope.

questions.explanation: An automatic (local) object is destroyed when control leaves the block `{ ... }` that defines it.

questions.statement: What is the primary motivation for defining inline methods in C++?

options.text: To guarantee that the compiler never creates a function call.
To allow a method to access private members of unrelated classes.
To avoid the runtime overhead of saving re-entry addresses and jumping to functions.
To defer all method compilation until the program is running.

questions.explanation: A normal call saves the return address, jumps to the function and jumps back. Inlining lets the compiler put the body at the call site instead. `inline` is only a hint, so the compiler may still generate a call.

questions.statement: Methods defined directly within the class body without using the `inline` keyword are known as _______ inline methods.

options.text: virtual
external
deferred
implicit

questions.explanation: A method whose body is written inside the class definition is implicitly inline, with no `inline` keyword needed.

questions.statement: Why must an explicit inline function's definition be available in the header file containing the class definition?

options.text: Because functions defined in headers are automatically private.
Because the compiler must have access to the code block of an inline function during compilation.
Because the linker cannot link functions that are defined in source files.
Because every header file is executed once at program startup.

questions.explanation: To expand an inline function where it is called, the compiler needs its body in every file that calls it, so the definition belongs in the header.

questions.statement: What is a major benefit of using access methods instead of placing data members directly in the public section?

options.text: Access methods make every data member globally accessible.
Access methods eliminate the need to define a class interface.
Access methods can prevent invalid access attempts by performing sanity checks.
Access methods guarantee that the class has no runtime cost.

questions.explanation: Getters and setters can validate values before they reach private data, so the object always stays in a valid state.

questions.statement: Why should a getter returning a string data member by reference return it as a `const` reference?

options.text: To prevent callers from writing directly to the private data member through the returned reference.
To force the getter to make a copy of the string every time.
To allow the getter to modify the string in a const object.
To make the string's lifetime extend beyond the lifetime of its object.

questions.explanation: Returning `const string&` avoids a copy and stops callers from modifying the private member through the reference.

questions.statement: If an object is declared `const`, what restriction does that place on method calls?

options.text: No methods, including constructors, can ever be called for the object.
Only static methods can be called for the object.
Every method called on the object becomes `const` automatically.
Only methods identified as read-only (`const`) can be called for this object.

questions.explanation: For a `const` object, the compiler only allows calls to methods declared `const` (read-only methods).

options.text: A constructor is not allowed to accept a `string` parameter.
`Account acc;` calls the destructor before the object has been constructed.
The class defines a constructor with a parameter, so no default constructor is generated, making `Account acc;` invalid.
A constructor must return `0` from `main`.

questions.explanation: `Account(string)` is a user-declared constructor, so there is no default constructor, and `Account acc;` has nothing to call.

options.text: Destructors cannot take any parameters.
A destructor must return `int`.
A destructor's name must be `delete Demo`.
A destructor must always be declared `static`.

questions.explanation: Destructors are called automatically, so there is nowhere to pass arguments from. A destructor cannot have parameters.

options.text: `void setName(const string& s) { if(s.empty()) return true; name = s; }`
`bool setName(const string& s) { if(s.size() < 1) return false; name = s; return true; }`
`bool setName(string s) { name = s; return false; }`
`bool setName() const { name.clear(); return true; }`

questions.explanation: Option A rejects an empty string, stores valid input and returns a `bool` on every path. `const string&` also avoids an unnecessary copy.

questions.statement:
A getter for a const object fails to compile because it lacks a required qualifier. How should it be fixed?

```cpp
unsigned long getNr() { return nr; }
```

options.text: `const unsigned long getNr(unsigned long nr) { return nr; }`
`unsigned long getNr() const { return nr; }`
`unsigned long const getNr() volatile { return nr; }`
`unsigned long getNr() static { return nr; }`

questions.explanation: Adding `const` after the parameter list makes `getNr()` a read-only method, so it can be called on const objects.

options.text: `void Book(string t, double p) { title = t; price = p; }`
`Book() { title = "Untitled"; price = 0.0; }`
`Book(const string& t = "Untitled") { title = t; }`
`Book(const string& t = "Untitled", double p = 0.0) { title = t; price = p; }`

questions.explanation: Default arguments let one constructor serve as `Book()`, `Book("C++")` and `Book("C++", 499.0)`.

options.text: `void DatabaseConnection() { }`
`DatabaseConnection::~() { }`
`~DatabaseConnection() { }`
`delete DatabaseConnection() { }`

questions.explanation: A destructor is `~ClassName()`, with no return type and no parameters.

questions.statement: If a class contains at least one constructor, a default constructor must be defined _______ if it is needed for uninitialized object creation.

options.text: explicitly
implicitly by the linker
after the destructor
only in a derived class

questions.explanation: When a class declares any constructor, a default constructor must be written explicitly (or requested with `= default`) if objects are created without arguments.

questions.statement:
`account` has a (non-`explicit`) constructor with one `string` parameter. What happens when this line is executed?

```cpp
account nomoney = string("Poor, Charles");
```

options.text: It always calls the default constructor first and then assigns the string.
It fails to compile because constructors cannot be used in copy-initialization.
It creates a pointer named `nomoney` that refers to a string literal.
It calls the one-parameter constructor, exactly like `account nomoney(string("Poor, Charles"));`.

questions.explanation: Copy-initialisation from a `string` uses the non-explicit converting constructor, so it behaves like direct initialisation. Note: `account nomoney = "Poor, Charles";` would NOT compile, because `const char*` to `string` to `account` needs two user-defined conversions.

options.text: `globalObject`
`localObject`
`temporaryObject`
`parameterObject`

questions.explanation: Global objects are constructed before `main()` starts and destroyed after it returns. Parameters and locals die when `f` returns, and temporaries at the end of their statement.

options.text: A method defined outside a class must always be declared `static`.
Methods cannot use `cout` inside a class.
It is an ordinary (non-inline) definition: add the `inline` keyword, or define the method inside the class body.
The method name must begin with a tilde to be defined outside the class.

questions.explanation: Without `inline`, this is an ordinary function definition. If the header is included in several `.cpp` files, the linker sees multiple definitions. Mark it `inline` or define it inside the class.

questions.statement:
Fix this accessor so it can be called on a const `Account` object.

```cpp
double getState() { return state; }
```

options.text: `const double getState(double state) { return state; }`
`double getState() const { return state; }`
`double getState() static { return state; }`
`void getState() const { return state; }`

questions.explanation: `const` after the parameter list makes `getState()` read-only, so const `Account` objects can call it.

options.text: `void getAge() { age = 0; }`
`int getAge(int age) { return age; }`
`int const getAge(int age) const { return age; }`
`int getAge() const { return age; }`

questions.explanation: A getter returns the member, takes no parameters and is `const` because it does not change the object.

questions.statement: Objects created by a constructor must be cleaned up in an orderly manner by a special method called a _______.

options.text: deallocator
destructor
finalizer function
constructor overload

questions.explanation: A destructor does the clean-up (freeing memory, closing files) when an object's lifetime ends.

questions.statement: What happens if a class does not define a destructor?

options.text: The class cannot be instantiated.
The compiler inserts a destructor that always deletes every pointer member.
The compiler creates a minimal version of a destructor as a public member, called the default destructor.
The object is never destroyed.

questions.explanation: Without a user-declared destructor, the compiler generates a public default destructor that destroys the members. It does not `delete` raw pointers the class owns.

questions.statement: Why can't the compiler determine whether a method performs write operations or only read operations unless additional information is supplied?

options.text: Member methods could potentially alter data members unless explicitly qualified as `const`.
All C++ methods are assumed to be `static` by default.
Private data members are invisible to the compiler.
Data members are always mutable, even in const objects.

questions.explanation: Unless a method is declared `const`, the compiler must assume it may modify data members, so it cannot be called on a const object.

questions.statement:
What is the error in this object definition if `Account` only has a constructor that accepts one `string` parameter?

```cpp
account somemoney("Li, Ed", 10.0);
```

options.text: The class does not contain a constructor with two parameters matching this signature.
Object names cannot contain the word `money`.
A string argument cannot be passed to a constructor.
Constructors cannot be called when defining objects.

questions.explanation: Two arguments are passed, but the only constructor takes one `string`. No constructor matches the call.

options.text: `const inline Account::display() { cout << name; }`
`inline void Account::display() { name = "Account holder"; }`
`void inline Account()::display const { cout << name; }`
`inline void Account::display() const { cout << "Account holder: " << name << endl; }`

questions.explanation: The definition must repeat the `const` from the declaration. Without it, it defines a different member function that the class never declared.

options.text: `void setState(double x) const { state = x; }`
`bool setState(double x) { if(x < 0) return false; state = x; return true; }`
`bool setState(double x) { state = x; return x < 0; }`
`double setState() { return state; }`

questions.explanation: Reject invalid input first, then update the member and return `true`.

questions.statement: To allow controlled access to private data members without compromising data encapsulation, programmers use _______ methods.

options.text: global
friend-only
access
allocation

questions.explanation: Access methods (getters and setters) give controlled access to private data without breaking encapsulation.

questions.statement: Which statement describes destruction order when an object contains another object as a data member?

options.text: Member object destructors are called in alphabetical order.
The containing object's destructor always runs after every member destructor.
Member object destructors are called in the reverse order of their creation.
Member object destructors are never called automatically.

questions.explanation: The containing object's destructor body runs first. Then its member objects are destroyed in the reverse order of their construction.

questions.statement:
What is wrong with this attempt to define a const object if `Account` only has a constructor requiring a `string` name?

```cpp
const Account inv;
```

options.text: Const objects cannot be instances of classes.
The `const` keyword can only be applied to pointers.
A const object must be allocated with `new`.
Const objects must be initialized when defined, and no default constructor is available.

questions.explanation: A const object must be initialised when it is defined. `const Account inv;` needs a default constructor, which `Account` does not have.

options.text: `Account::Account(const string& a_name, unsigned long a_nr, double a_state) { name = a_name; nr = a_nr; state = a_state; }`
`void Account::Account(string& a_name, unsigned long a_nr, double a_state) { name = a_name; nr = a_nr; state = a_state; }`
`Account::Account(const string& a_name) { name = a_name; nr = a_nr; state = a_state; }`
`Account::Account(string a_name, unsigned long a_nr, double a_state) const { name = a_name; nr = a_nr; state = a_state; }`

questions.explanation: `const string&` avoids copying the string and promises not to change it. Constructors never have a return type or a trailing `const`.

questions.statement: Which complete inline getter returns a read-only reference to a private `string name` member and is const-qualified?

options.text: `string& getName() { return name; }`
`const string& getName() const { return name; }`
`const string getName(const string& name) { return name; }`
`void getName() const { return name; }`

questions.explanation: `const string&` avoids a copy and blocks modification, and the trailing `const` lets const objects call the getter.

questions.statement: Methods that perform only read operations and need to be called for constant objects must be identified as _______.

options.text: virtual
static-only
immutable-returning
read-only

questions.explanation: Read-only methods (declared `const` after the parameter list) are the only methods a const object can call.

questions.statement: What is a primary advantage of modifying a class's internal data structures while keeping its public interface unchanged through access methods?

options.text: Application programs using the class can be updated by simply recompiling without modifying the application code itself.
Applications no longer need to link against the class implementation.
The class's private data automatically becomes public.
Existing binaries are guaranteed to work without recompilation after any internal change.

questions.explanation: Because the public interface stays the same, programs that use the class only need to be recompiled, not rewritten.

questions.statement: A program has already created an object named `nomoney` and then tries to invoke that object's constructor explicitly again. Why does this cause a compilation error?

options.text: Constructors can only be called on pointers.
An object can only be created inside a destructor.
Constructors cannot be called explicitly for an existing object (`nomoney`).
An object named `nomoney` must have static storage duration.

questions.explanation: A constructor runs exactly once, when the object is created. To change an existing object, use assignment or a setter.

options.text: Change `~Item() {}` to `~Item(unsigned long nr) {}`.
Change `unsigned long getNr() { return nr; }` to `unsigned long getNr() const { return nr; }`.
Remove the default value from `Item(unsigned long n = 0)`.
Change `nr` to a public static member.

questions.explanation: `getNr()` does not modify the object. Marking it `const` lets const `Item` objects call it.
